lab_title: Vectors and Projectile Motion: From Components to Trajectories
top_level_objectives: Represent physical quantities as vectors with magnitude and direction
Add vectors tip-to-tail to find a resultant
Decompose a vector into perpendicular (x and y) components using trigonometry
Relate a vector's magnitude and direction to its components
Apply vector decomposition to the initial velocity of a projectile
Recognize that horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent
Predict how launch angle and speed affect trajectory, range, and maximum height

scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce vectors as arrows encoding both magnitude and direction, distinguishing them from scalars, in a floating AR workspace.
key_visuals: Several labeled arrows of different lengths and orientations floating in space
A scalar quantity (e.g., a plain number/temperature readout) shown beside a vector arrow for contrast
Grid with x and y axes for reference
student_actions: Rotate and inspect vector arrows from different viewing angles
Drag a vector arrow to change its length and direction
Match vectors to real-world examples (e.g., velocity vs. speed) via a simple sorting task

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate how two vectors combine graphically to form a resultant vector using the tip-to-tail method.
key_visuals: Two colored vector arrows (A and B) that can be dragged
Animated ghost copy of vector B sliding to the tip of vector A
Resultant vector C drawn from the tail of A to the tip of B, highlighted in a third color
student_actions: Drag vectors A and B to different orientations and magnitudes
Trigger the tip-to-tail animation to see the resultant form
Predict the resultant's approximate length and direction before revealing it

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how any single vector can be broken into perpendicular x and y components, connecting the geometry to right-triangle trigonometry.
key_visuals: A single vector arrow overlaid on an x-y grid
Dashed projection lines dropping to the x-axis and y-axis showing the component vectors
Right triangle formed by the vector and its components, with angle theta labeled
Live-updating readout of magnitude, angle, and component values
student_actions: Rotate the vector using a handle and watch the components update in real time
Use sliders for magnitude and angle to see how components change
Compute components by hand for a given angle and check against the displayed values

scenes.scene_name: From Components Back to Magnitude and Direction
scenes.brief_purpose: Reinforce the reversible relationship between components and the original vector using the Pythagorean theorem and inverse trigonometric functions.
key_visuals: Two perpendicular component arrows (x and y) placed on the grid
A reconstructed resultant vector drawn from summing the components
Formula overlay showing magnitude = sqrt(x^2+y^2) and angle = arctan(y/x)
student_actions: Input or adjust component values with sliders
Predict the resulting magnitude and angle before the overlay reveals the calculation
Toggle between 'decompose' and 'recompose' modes to see the inverse operations

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition from abstract vectors to a physical scenario by introducing a projectile with an initial velocity vector at a chosen angle and speed.
key_visuals: A launcher (e.g., a small cannon) sitting on a horizontal ground plane
Initial velocity vector shown at the launch point, decomposed into horizontal and vertical components
Angle slider and speed slider with live-updating vector display
student_actions: Adjust launch angle and initial speed using sliders
Observe how the velocity vector and its components change shape before firing
Fire the projectile and watch it follow a parabolic path

scenes.scene_name: Independence of Horizontal and Vertical Motion
scenes.brief_purpose: Highlight the core insight that horizontal velocity stays constant while vertical velocity changes uniformly under gravity, and that these two motions are independent.
key_visuals: Side-by-side velocity component arrows attached to the moving projectile, updating each frame
A horizontal 'shadow' projectile moving at constant velocity and a vertical 'shadow' projectile under free-fall, launched simultaneously for comparison
Graphs of horizontal velocity (flat line) and vertical velocity (linearly changing line) over time
student_actions: Play the launch in slow motion and pause at multiple points to inspect the component vectors
Compare the real projectile's horizontal position to the constant-velocity shadow object
Compare the real projectile's vertical position to the free-fall shadow object

scenes.brief_purpose: Let students experiment with launch angle and speed to see how they determine the trajectory's range and maximum height, building intuition for optimal launch conditions.
key_visuals: Trajectory trace lines left behind after each launch, color-coded by angle
Live readouts of range, maximum height, and time of flight
Marker showing the 45-degree angle trajectory for comparison against other angles
student_actions: Launch multiple projectiles at different angles while keeping speed constant, comparing ranges
Launch multiple projectiles at different speeds while keeping angle constant, comparing heights and ranges
Try to identify the launch angle that maximizes range through guided trial and error

scenes.brief_purpose: Assess and consolidate understanding by having students use vector reasoning to hit a specified target using an appropriate launch angle and speed.
key_visuals: A target marker placed at a specific horizontal distance on the ground
Vector decomposition overlay available on demand as a hint
Success/failure feedback animation when the projectile lands relative to the target
student_actions: Calculate or estimate the required launch angle and speed to hit the target
Enter values and launch the projectile
Adjust based on feedback and relaunch until the target is hit, then explain their reasoning using vector components
